Baby & Child

Dandy–Walker malformation: signs, diagnosis and care

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hearing an unfamiliar name after a brain scan can leave a family with many questions. Dandy–Walker malformation is a difference in brain development that begins before birth. Its effects vary considerably. Understanding the precise scan findings, whether fluid pressure is increasing and whether other conditions are present helps the care team explain what comes next.

What changes in the developing brain?

Dandy–Walker malformation involves the cerebellum, at the back of the brain, and its relationship with nearby fluid spaces. The cerebellum helps coordinate movement and balance and also contributes to thinking and behaviour. The vermis is the middle portion joining its two sides. In Dandy–Walker malformation, this part is underdeveloped and its shape and position are altered.

The fourth ventricle is a cerebrospinal-fluid cavity between the brainstem and cerebellum. Traditional descriptions combine changes in the vermis with an enlarged, cyst-like fourth ventricle and a large posterior fossa, the space in the skull containing these structures. Modern imaging work places greater weight on the detailed anatomy of the vermis and nearby tissues; an enlarged posterior fossa is not a necessary finding in the refined definition.

Some children also develop hydrocephalus, meaning an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid. Fluid circulation can be disrupted and pressure can rise inside the skull. In a baby, this may make the head grow unusually quickly. Hydrocephalus needs its own assessment and treatment; the diagnosis of Dandy–Walker malformation alone does not tell a family whether it is present.

Signs, development and the range of outcomes

Possible signs include slower progress with movement skills, reduced muscle tone or later muscle stiffness, poor coordination and difficulty with balance. A child may need extra support to sit, move around or walk. The combination and severity of difficulties differ, so another family’s experience may not describe your child’s needs.

Learning and intellectual development also vary. Intellectual disability is not inevitable, and a child without it can still have specific learning needs. Other brain differences, a chromosome condition and complications from hydrocephalus can affect the overall outlook. Follow-up should assess the child’s abilities and progress rather than assume a fixed outcome from the diagnostic name.

Seizures can occur. Severe pressure-related problems may also affect essential brain functions, including breathing, which is why concerning symptoms need urgent attention. Some children are diagnosed in pregnancy or infancy, while others come to medical attention later. Timing depends partly on the symptoms, associated conditions and when hydrocephalus appears; a later diagnosis does not by itself establish how much support will be needed.

Why the exact diagnosis matters

Reports may mention cerebellar vermian hypoplasia, meaning a small or incompletely developed vermis, or mega cisterna magna, an enlarged fluid space behind the cerebellum. These findings can resemble aspects of Dandy–Walker malformation on a scan, especially before birth. They should be described carefully rather than treated as interchangeable labels.

In isolated vermian hypoplasia, the vermis is small without necessarily having the characteristic arrangement of structures seen in Dandy–Walker malformation. Older reports sometimes use “Dandy–Walker variant”, a broad term that can obscure the actual anatomy. Ask the specialist to explain which structures are affected and whether the diagnosis is definite or still being clarified.

Mega cisterna magna generally describes an enlarged cisterna magna with otherwise normal brain structures. It is not simply a more severe Dandy–Walker malformation. Clinicians check whether the finding is truly isolated and may recommend further imaging or follow-up. There is no reliable universal ranking in which every child with one of these labels will do better or worse than every child with another. Associated findings and diagnostic certainty matter.

Possible causes and associated conditions

The underlying difference arises during early development of the cerebellum and surrounding structures. A genetic or chromosome change is identified in some children, while in many others the cause remains uncertain. A diagnosis does not establish that a parent caused the condition through an ordinary activity, meal or emotion during pregnancy.

Reported chromosome findings include deletions involving the 3q24 region containing ZIC1 and ZIC4, changes involving 6p25 or parts of 13q, and duplication of 9p. These are examples from affected individuals, not a complete diagnostic checklist or a test result that every child will have. The size and content of a chromosome change and the child’s other findings affect its interpretation.

Some children have a wider pattern of differences. One recognised association is PHACE, which can involve a large infantile haemangioma, differences in brain or artery development, heart or aortic abnormalities and eye findings. Sternal or other midline defects may also occur, and the name PHACES is sometimes used. This association is a reason for coordinated assessment when relevant features are present, not a reason to assume every child with Dandy–Walker malformation has PHACE.

Complex genetic and environmental influences have been proposed for other cases. Often a single explanation cannot be established. Broad claims that most associated syndromes are actually a different malformation are also difficult to apply to an individual family: the team needs to interpret the imaging and genetic information together.

What this means for another pregnancy

Many affected children have no family history of the condition. When a specific genetic condition is identified, the chance of recurrence depends on that condition and its inheritance. A genetic counsellor can review the child’s results, the family history and whether testing of either parent would be useful.

A single percentage cannot represent all families. Estimates quoted for apparently isolated cases are not automatically suitable when two siblings are affected, when another syndrome is present or when the scan diagnosis is uncertain. A 25% recurrence figure may apply to some confirmed autosomal recessive conditions; it should not be assigned to every family with Dandy–Walker malformation or to all X-linked conditions. Ask for a risk estimate tied to the actual diagnosis, including what remains unknown.

How diagnosis works before and after birth

Ultrasound during pregnancy may raise the first concern. A detailed fetal brain examination, called neurosonography, helps define the anatomy; fetal MRI may add useful information. Repeat imaging can help clarify findings as the pregnancy progresses. A specialist also looks for differences elsewhere in the baby’s body and discusses whether genetic testing, including testing through amniocentesis, is appropriate.

After birth, examination and brain imaging help confirm the diagnosis and assess fluid spaces. Ultrasound, MRI or CT may be used depending on the clinical question and urgency; they are not equivalent tests that parents need to arrange themselves. MRI provides detailed anatomy, while CT may be selected in particular postnatal circumstances. Mentioning CT here does not mean it is a routine fetal screening test.

Useful questions include: what is the precise diagnosis, is hydrocephalus present, are there other findings, and what follow-up is planned? If the diagnosis is made before birth, discuss the birth setting and access to the specialists who will assess the baby. Imaging can guide these decisions but cannot predict every aspect of later development.

Treatment and ongoing support

Care addresses the child’s complications and developmental needs. When hydrocephalus needs surgery, a neurosurgeon may place a shunt to divert fluid to another part of the body where it can be absorbed. An endoscopic procedure may be an option for selected children, depending on their anatomy. The specialist decides which approach is suitable.

Surgery for fluid pressure does not reconstruct the cerebellum. Continuing care may include physiotherapy, learning support, other medical treatment and help with everyday participation. Social services and, later, educational or vocational support can be part of the plan. Families should be involved in choosing practical goals that matter in their child’s daily life.

A child with a shunt needs follow-up because blockage or infection can develop. Ask for a clear written plan for concerning symptoms and whom to contact, including outside normal clinic hours. Genetic counselling remains useful even when no cause is found, since it can explain the limits of testing and options for future pregnancies.

When to seek urgent help

Seek prompt medical assessment for possible hydrocephalus symptoms, such as a tense or bulging soft spot, unusually rapid head growth, persistently downward-looking eyes, repeated vomiting, poor feeding or unusual sleepiness. In a child already receiving treatment, new or returning symptoms should be discussed urgently with the treating service.

Call local emergency services if a child has severe breathing difficulty, is unresponsive or is very difficult to wake. Do not wait for the next scheduled scan or appointment when a child appears seriously unwell. The care team can give more specific instructions for seizures and for the child’s individual treatment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Specialist imaging helps separate Dandy–Walker malformation from other posterior-fossa findings; the name alone is insufficient to predict outcome.

Genetic counselling and assessment for associated conditions help make recurrence discussions specific to the family.

Fluid pressure and developmental needs require continuing clinical assessment; surgery is chosen for the individual child.

How BeMama can help

Keep the scan report, test results and care contacts together. Bring a short list of questions about the exact diagnosis, follow-up and the next practical step for your family.

When to seek help

This article cannot interpret a scan or predict a child’s development. Seek urgent help for concerning new neurological symptoms and emergency help for severe breathing difficulty or reduced responsiveness.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Dandy–Walker malformation begins before birth and has a wide range of effects.
  • Hydrocephalus is an associated problem that requires separate assessment.
  • Similar scan terms do not necessarily describe the same condition or outlook.
  • A family-specific genetic assessment is more useful than a universal recurrence percentage.
  • Ongoing developmental support and a clear urgent-care plan matter alongside imaging.

Frequently asked questions

Does every child with Dandy–Walker malformation have an intellectual disability?

No. Cognitive outcomes vary, and learning difficulties and intellectual disability are not identical. The care team considers other findings, complications and the child’s progress when discussing support and outlook.

What signs can Dandy–Walker malformation cause?

Possible features include delayed movement skills, low or increased muscle tone, coordination or balance difficulties and seizures. Hydrocephalus may cause additional symptoms such as rapid head growth, vomiting or unusual sleepiness. Some children have relatively few symptoms.

How is the diagnosis confirmed?

A specialist interprets brain imaging together with the clinical findings. Ultrasound, MRI and sometimes CT have different roles. The report should distinguish Dandy–Walker malformation from other cerebellar and fluid-space findings.

Can it be detected during pregnancy?

Yes, ultrasound may identify concerning anatomy and a detailed specialist scan or fetal MRI may clarify it. Follow-up imaging and discussion of associated findings and genetic testing are often part of the assessment.

Is mega cisterna magna a more severe form of Dandy–Walker malformation?

No. It describes a different fluid-space finding, generally with otherwise normal brain structures. Confirming whether it is isolated is important; the name should not be used to predict a uniformly worse outcome.

Will surgery cure the underlying malformation?

Treatment can relieve hydrocephalus when present, but it does not rebuild the cerebellum. The child may still benefit from developmental, educational and other support tailored to their needs.

Could a future baby also be affected?

The answer depends on the underlying cause and family findings. Ask a genetic counsellor for an individual estimate rather than applying a general figure such as 5% or 25% to your family.

What should we bring to the next appointment?

Bring the imaging report, available genetic results, a record of new symptoms and your current care plan. Ask which findings are confirmed, what is still uncertain, and whom to contact urgently if symptoms change.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
